claim_details.claim: The comparison of prolonged sitting to smoking is a subject of genuine scientific debate. On one hand, many medical experts consider the health risks of prolonged sedentary behavior—increased risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease even depression—comparable to those caused by smoking , with one expert arguing that cumulative damage from prolonged sitting can be equated to the negative health consequences of smoking ; a prominent researcher has even described sitting as 'more dangerous than smoking,' though acknowledges that some disagree

On the other hand, peer-reviewed research published in the American Journal of Public Health concludes that while excessive sitting (roughly more than eight hours a day) does increase the risk of premature death and chronic diseases by 10–20%, this risk pale[s] in comparison to the roughly 180% increased risk of premature death associated with smoking a separate study notes that the economic and mortality burden of smoking far exceeds that of physical inactivity

Additionally, critics argue that the analogy is misleading because sitting itself is not inherently harmful—it is the accompanying inactivity that drives health risks as little as 60–75 minutes of moderate exercise per day can offset the harms of 8 hours of sedentary behavior

Overall, while sedentary lifestyle is recognized as a significant public health concern, the framing of 'sitting is the new smoking' remains contested, with experts and researchers holding opposing views on the accuracy of the comparison

claim_details.claim: The question of whether pregnant women should follow a vegan diet is subject to genuine disagreement among medical authorities. claim_details.claim: The Word of Wisdom became mandatory in multiple senses across different timeframes. It was first announced as a revelation in 1833 but was not initially given as a commandment ; rather, it was described as 'not by commandment or constraint, but by revelation'

In 1851, President Brigham Young proposed to the general conference that all Church members formally covenant to keep the Word of Wisdom this proposal was unanimously accepted, at which point it became binding as a commandment for all Church members

By 1915–1919, the First Presidency under President Heber J. Grant made strict Word of Wisdom observance a requirement for receiving a temple recommend and for priesthood ordination it remains a distinguishing hallmark of LDS society today
